newsitem.title: ITALY: Stet, IBM deal falls short of early hopes.
newsitem.headline: Stet, IBM deal falls short of early hopes.

text.p: Italian telecom holding Stet has finally completed its long awaited co-operation deal with U.S. computer giant IBM, but the accord was less substantial than many commentators expected.
Stet and IBM announced the joint venture late on Friday, some 16 months after proposals for a deal were first unveiled, saying the firms would market each others' products worldwide.

While Stet was relieved it had managed to agree terms with such a prestigious partner, the accord fell short of the wide-ranging relationship many in the market had hoped for, putting pressure on the group's management at a delicate moment.
"The (hoped for) exchange of stategy and people with IBM has basically turned into a commercial venture," the respected financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore wrote at the weekend.

The joint marketing deal, which will become operative as soon as it has been approved by anti-trust authorities, includes promotion of computing, networking, information technology, Internet and voice and data services.

Stet said it hoped the project would develop further, but as things stand the Rome-based holding, Europe's fourth-biggest phone company which is due to be privatised next year, looks increasingly isolated in its main, telecommunications market.
"While all the other bigs in the telecommunications field are getting married, Stet is the only world player to remain a spinster," Corriere della Sera newspaper said at the weekend.
"After 16 months of talks (with IBM) the mountain has given way to a molehill," it added.

Hours before announcing the IBM agreement, Stet said in a statement that it was expecting consolidated net profits of 3.0 trillion lire ($2.0 billion) in 1996 against 2.452 trillion in 1995. It added that group sales should be more than 40 trillion lire, a rise of eight percent on the previous year.

Much of Stet's profit's come from its fixed-line operator Telecom Italia, which operates a virtual monopoly at home. But this cash cow might come under threat from 1998 once the telecom market is deregulated and competitors from other European Union countries are allowed to muscle into Italy.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition government announced last month that it planned to fuse Stet with Telecom Italia ahead of the much-delayed sell-off.
It is now facing calls to give Telecom Italia management the upper hand following the merger.

"We need an operating company that is capable of making strategic choices in the field. In this, Telecom has greater know-how than Stet," said Andrea Margheri, industry spokesman for government ally the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS).
As a first step towards an eventual shake-up, the Treasury took direct control of Stet from debt-troubled state holding IRI on Friday.
One of the first things the Treasury is expected to do is replace IRI representatives on the Stet board.
"This might give management a new dynamism even in the field of international alliances of which Stet has great need," Il Sole 24 Ore wrote.
